subject: maths
title: Data, Tables and Graphs: Sorting, Tally Marks, Picture Graphs and Column Graphs
seo_title: Year 2 Data and Graphs Worksheets: Sorting, Tally Marks, Tables and Column Graphs (Free, with Answer Key)
standard_text: Acquire data for categorical variables through surveys, observation, experiment and using digital tools; sort data into relevant categories and display data using lists and tables
meta_desc: Free Year 2 maths worksheets on data for the Australian Curriculum: sorting objects into groups, tally marks and tables, picture graphs and column graphs with a scale of 1, and “how many more?” questions. 100 questions with an answer key.
key_big: Sort by one rule, count carefully, then read the table or graph.
key_sub: The 5th tally mark goes across the other four. In a picture graph one picture is 1. Altogether means add; how many more means take away.
body_html:
What is data?

Data is information we collect. We can ask a question, such as “What is your favourite sport?”, or we can look and count, such as birds in the schoolyard. Then we sort the data into groups and show it in a table or a graph.

Sort into groups

Choose one rule, such as colour, shape or size. Every object goes into one group only.

Tally marks and tables

Draw one mark for each thing. The 5th mark goes across the other four. Count the groups in 5s, then count on the single marks. Write the number in the table.

Example

How many students chose netball?

1 group of 5 is 5. Then 1 more: 6.

Answer: 6 students

Picture graphs

In a picture graph, one picture stands for one thing. Count the pictures in each row. The longest row is the most.

Column graphs

Find the label at the bottom. Go up to the top of its column, then across to the numbers. Each line stands for 1. The tallest column is the most.

The table, the picture graph and the column graph above all show the same data.

Add or take away?

The question saysDo this
altogether, in total, both, A or BAdd
how many more, how many fewer, differenceTake away
Example

How many more students chose AFL than soccer?

AFL 7, soccer 3. 7 − 3 = 4.

Answer: 4 more students

Common mistakes

MistakeWhat to do instead
Counting a group of 5 tally marks as 4The line across is the 5th mark
Drawing 5 lines and then a line acrossDraw 4 lines, then the 5th goes across
Sorting by colour when the rule is shapeRead the rule, and look only at that
Reading the row or column next to the right onePut your finger on the label first
Adding when the question says how many moreHow many more means take away

faq.q: What do Year 2 students learn about data in the Australian Curriculum?
faq.a: They collect data with surveys and by counting, sort it into categories and record it in lists and tables. They also make and compare simple displays such as picture graphs and column graphs.

faq.q: How do you teach tally marks in Year 2?
faq.a: Draw one mark for each thing and draw the 5th mark across the other four. Students then count the groups in 5s and count on the single marks: 2 groups and 3 marks is 13.

faq.q: What is the difference between a picture graph and a column graph?
faq.a: A picture graph uses a picture for each thing, so you count the pictures. A column graph uses columns, so you read the top of each column against the numbers on the side.
No. NAPLAN starts in Year 3. Reading tables and graphs in Year 2 builds the skills students use later in Year 3.

items.q: How many triangles are there?
items.e: A triangle has 3 sides and 3 corners. Touch each triangle once and count: 1, 2, 3, 4. There are 4 triangles. Count only triangles, not the other shapes.

items.q: How many red shapes are there?
items.e: Look at the colour only. Count every red shape, whatever its shape: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. There are 6 red shapes.

items.q: How many blue triangles are there?
items.e: The shape must be a triangle and it must be blue. There are 4 triangles, but only 2 of them are blue.

items.q: How many big shapes are there?
items.e: Look at the size only. Count the big shapes: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. There are 7 big shapes. (5 shapes are small.)

items.q: Sort the shapes by shape. Which group has the most?
items.e: Count each group: circles 5, squares 4, stars 3. The biggest number is 5, so circles is the biggest group.

items.q: How many shapes are not yellow?
items.e: Not yellow means every other colour. Here that is the green shapes: 1, 2, 3. Check: 12 shapes − 9 yellow = 3.

items.q: Mia sorts these shapes by colour. How many groups will she make?
items.e: Mia makes one group for each colour: red, blue and yellow. That is 3 groups. (4 groups would be sorting by shape: circles, triangles, squares and stars.)

items.q: Noah sorts the same shapes by shape. How many groups will he make?
items.e: Noah makes one group for each kind of shape: circles, triangles, squares and stars. That is 4 groups. (3 groups would be sorting by colour.)

items.q: How were these shapes sorted?
items.e: Group 1 has only circles, Group 2 only stars and Group 3 only squares. The colours and sizes are mixed. So they are sorted by shape.

items.q: How were these shapes sorted?
items.e: Group 1 has only red shapes. Group 2 has only blue shapes. The shapes and the sizes are mixed. So they are sorted by colour.

items.q: How were these shapes sorted?
items.e: Group 1 has only big shapes. Group 2 has only small shapes. The shapes and colours are mixed. So they are sorted by size.

items.q: Which shape is in the wrong group?
items.e: Read the label on each group. Check every lettered shape. Shape C is a circle. It belongs in the Circles group. The other lettered shapes are in the right group.

items.q: Which shape is in the wrong group?
items.e: Read the label on each group. Check every lettered shape. Shape A is blue. It belongs in the Blue group. The other lettered shapes are in the right group.

items.q: Which shape is in the wrong group?
items.e: Read the label on each group. Check every lettered shape. Shape D is big. It belongs in the Big group. The other lettered shapes are in the right group.

items.q: Charlotte sorts the shapes by shape. What number goes in the table for triangles?
items.e: Count the triangles of every colour: 1, 2. So 2 goes in the table. Check: 4 + 2 + 7 = 13 shapes.

items.q: Then Charlotte sorts the same shapes by colour. What number goes in the table for yellow?
items.e: Count every yellow shape: 1, 2, 3, 4. So 4 goes in the table. Check: 3 + 6 + 4 = 13 shapes, the same as before.

items.q: Kai sorts these shapes into two groups: shapes with corners and shapes with no corners. How many shapes have no corners?
items.e: Only circles have no corners. Count the circles: 1, 2, 3. So 3 shapes have no corners. The other 9 shapes have corners.

items.q: Oliver has 16 toy cars. He sorts them into red cars and cars that are not red. 7 cars are red. How many cars are not red?
items.e: All the cars are in one group or the other. 16 − 7 = 9 cars are not red. (Adding gives 23, but there are only 16 cars.)

items.q: Ava sorts her shells into big shells and small shells. She has 6 big shells and 8 small shells. How many shells does she have altogether?
items.e: Altogether means add the two groups: 6 + 8 = 14 shells. (2 is how many more small shells than big shells.)

items.q: Lunch boxes in 2C have 20 items. 8 are fruit, 5 are sandwiches and the rest are snacks. How many snacks are there?
items.e: Step 1: fruit and sandwiches: 8 + 5 = 13. Step 2: 20 − 13 = 7 snacks. (13 is the fruit and sandwiches, not the snacks.)

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Four lines with one line across make a group of 5. 1 group of 5 and 1 more. Count 5, then 6. So it is 6.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Four lines with one line across make a group of 5. 1 group of 5 and 4 more. Count 5, then 6, 7, 8, 9. So it is 9.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Four lines with one line across make a group of 5. 2 groups of 5 and 2 more. Count 5, 10, then 11, 12. So it is 12.

items.q: What number do these tally marks show?
items.e: Four lines with one line across make a group of 5. 3 groups of 5 and 2 more. Count 5, 10, 15, then 16, 17. So it is 17.
12 = 5 + 5 + 2. Look for 2 groups of 5 and 2 single marks. That is C. A shows 17 (one group of 5 too many); B shows 11 (one mark too few); D shows 13 (one mark too many).

items.q: Zara has drawn 4 tally marks. How should she draw the 5th mark?
c: A line next to the 4 marks
items.e: The 5th mark goes across the other four. This makes a group of 5 that is easy to count in 5s.

items.q: What number goes in the Number column for Mango?
items.e: Mango has 2 groups of 5 and 1 more. Count 5, 10, then 11. So 11 goes in the table.

items.q: Which fruit got the fewest votes?
items.e: Grapes has only 3 marks and no group of 5. That is fewer than Banana (5), Apple (8) and Mango (11).

items.q: How many more votes did Apple get than Banana?
items.e: Apple 8, Banana 5. How many more means take away: 8 − 5 = 3. (13 is 8 + 5, the votes altogether.)

items.q: How many votes were there altogether?
items.e: First find Mango: 11. Then add every row: 8 + 5 + 11 + 3 = 27. (Counting each group of 5 as 4 gives 23. Leaving out Mango gives 16.)

items.q: How many days were rainy?
items.e: Put your finger on Rainy. Go across to the Days column. It says 3. (4 is the row above, Cloudy.)

items.q: Which weather did we have most often?
items.e: The biggest number in the Days column is 6, next to Sunny.

items.q: How many more sunny days than rainy days were there?
items.e: Sunny 6, rainy 3. How many more means take away: 6 − 3 = 3. (9 is 6 + 3.)

items.q: How many days were not sunny?
items.e: Not sunny means cloudy, rainy or windy: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8 days. Check: 14 days − 6 sunny days = 8.

items.q: Noah asked his friends, “What pet do you have?” He wrote: dog, cat, dog, fish, dog, cat, dog, dog, cat, fish, dog, rabbit. How many tally marks should go next to Dog?
items.e: Cross off each “dog” as you count it: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. Draw a group of 5 and 1 more mark. (12 is all the answers, and 3 is the cats.)

items.q: Here are Noah’s answers again: dog, cat, dog, fish, dog, cat, dog, dog, cat, fish, dog, rabbit. Which pet did only one friend have?
items.e: Count each pet: dog 6, cat 3, fish 2, rabbit 1. Only one friend has a rabbit.

items.q: There are 25 students in the survey. How many students ride a bike?
items.e: Add the rows we know: 7 + 9 + 4 = 20. Then 25 − 20 = 5. Check the tally: Bike has 1 group of 5. So 5 students ride a bike.

items.q: How many more students come by car than walk?
items.e: Car 9, walk 7. How many more means take away: 9 − 7 = 2. (16 is 9 + 7.)

items.q: Jack counts the cars going past the school gate. He draws 3 groups of 5 and 2 more marks. How many cars did he count?
items.e: Count the groups in 5s: 5, 10, 15. Then 2 more: 16, 17. So 17 cars. (Counting each group as 4 gives 14.)

items.q: Ruby counted 13 votes for netball. How should she draw the tally?
items.e: 13 = 5 + 5 + 3. Draw 2 groups of 5, then 3 single marks. Never leave 5 single marks: make another group of 5. (3 groups and 2 marks is 17.)

sets.title: Picture graphs: one picture for each

items.q: How many votes did the kangaroo get?
items.e: Each circle stands for 1 vote. Put your finger on the Kangaroo row and count the circles: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. So 7 votes. (Make sure you count the right row.)
Each star stands for 1 bird. Put your finger on the Lorikeet row and count the stars: 1, 2, 3, 4. So 4 birds. (Make sure you count the right row.)

items.q: Which row has the most books?
items.e: Each square stands for 1, so the longest row has the most. Isla has 7 squares. Others: Charlotte 5, Jack 2, Oliver 4.

items.q: How many students chose AFL?
items.e: Each circle stands for 1 student. Put your finger on the AFL row and count the circles: 1, 2, 3, 4. So 4 students. (Make sure you count the right row.)
Each star stands for 1, so the shortest row has the fewest. Banana has 4 stars. Others: Mango 7, Orange 5, Apple 6.

items.q: Which row shows 2 ice blocks?
items.e: Count the squares in each row. The Fri row has 2, so it shows 2 ice blocks.

items.q: How many students walk to school?
items.e: Each circle stands for 1 student. Put your finger on the Walk row and count the circles: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6. So 6 students. (Make sure you count the right row.)
Ruby: 6. Zara: 2. How many more means find the difference: 6 − 2 = 4. You can also match the stars in the two rows and count the extra ones. (Adding gives 8.)

items.q: Which row shows 9 votes?
items.e: Count the squares in each row. The Pink row has 9, so it shows 9 votes.

items.q: How many fewer students have a dog than a rabbit?
items.e: Dog: 1. Rabbit: 9. How many fewer means find the difference: 9 − 1 = 8. You can also match the circles in the two rows and count the extra ones. (Adding gives 10.)
Walk: 4. Bus: 2. How many more means find the difference: 4 − 2 = 2. You can also match the stars in the two rows and count the extra ones. (Adding gives 6.)

items.q: How many ice blocks were sold on Thursday and Wednesday altogether?
items.e: Thu: 6. Wed: 2. Altogether means add: 6 + 2 = 8 ice blocks.

items.q: Which row has the most votes?
items.e: Each circle stands for 1, so the longest row has the most. Wombat has 9 circles. Others: Kangaroo 1, Koala 5, Echidna 7, Emu 2.
Each star stands for 1 vote. Put your finger on the Red row and count the stars: 1. So 1 vote. (Make sure you count the right row.)

items.q: How many more students chose AFL than soccer?
items.e: AFL: 6. Soccer: 2. How many more means find the difference: 6 − 2 = 4. You can also match the squares in the two rows and count the extra ones. (Adding gives 8.)

items.q: Which row shows 3 books?
items.e: Count the circles in each row. The Mia row has 3, so it shows 3 books.
Count every row: Mango 9, Apple 5, Banana 3, Grapes 8. Add them: 9 + 5 + 3 + 8 = 25 votes.

items.q: Which row has the fewest students?
items.e: Each square stands for 1, so the shortest row has the fewest. Bird has 1 square. Others: Cat 6, Dog 5, Rabbit 8.

items.q: How many more shells did Zara find than Kai?
items.e: Zara: 6. Kai: 1. How many more means find the difference: 6 − 1 = 5. You can also match the circles in the two rows and count the extra ones. (Adding gives 7.)
Count every row: Ibis 3, Galah 9, Magpie 4, Lorikeet 1. Add them: 3 + 9 + 4 + 1 = 17 birds.

sets.title: Column graphs with a scale of 1

items.q: How many votes did Mango get?
items.e: Find Mango at the bottom. Go up to the top of that column, then across to the numbers. It ends on the line for 7. So 7 votes. (Use the column above the label, not the one next to it.)

items.q: How many students walk to school?
items.e: Find Walk at the bottom. Go up to the top of that column, then across to the numbers. It ends on the line for 8. So 8 students. (Use the column above the label, not the one next to it.)

items.q: The numbers on the side go 0, 1, 2, 3 … How many does each line stand for?
items.e: Each line is 1 more than the line below it, so each line stands for 1.

items.q: Which column shows the most votes?
items.e: The tallest column shows the most. The Emu column is 7 high.

items.q: How many books did Mia read?
items.e: Find Mia at the bottom. Go up to the top of that column, then across to the numbers. It ends on the line for 8. So 8 books. (Use the column above the label, not the one next to it.)

items.q: Which column shows 6 students?
items.e: Find 6 on the side. Go across the line for 6. The Bird column ends on that line.

items.q: Which column shows the fewest ice blocks?
items.e: The shortest column shows the fewest. The Thu column is 2 high.

items.q: How many ibises did the class see?
items.e: Find Ibis at the bottom. Go up to the top of that column, then across to the numbers. It ends on the line for 6. So 6 birds. (Use the column above the label, not the one next to it.)

items.q: Which column shows 1 vote?
items.e: Find 1 on the side. Go across the line for 1. The Green column ends on that line.

items.q: How many more students chose soccer than netball?
items.e: Soccer: 7. Netball: 5. How many more means find the difference: 7 − 5 = 2. (Adding gives 12, but that is how many altogether.)

items.q: How many votes did Grapes get?
items.e: Find Grapes at the bottom. Go up to the top of that column, then across to the numbers. It ends on the line for 6. So 6 votes. (Use the column above the label, not the one next to it.)

items.q: How many more ice blocks were sold on Tuesday than on Wednesday?
items.e: Tue: 8. Wed: 6. How many more means find the difference: 8 − 6 = 2. (Adding gives 14, but that is how many altogether.)

items.q: How many students chose soccer or cricket?
items.e: Soccer: 8. Cricket: 5. Altogether means add: 8 + 5 = 13 students. (3 is the difference.)

items.q: How many fewer votes did purple get than red?
items.e: Purple: 5. Red: 9. How many fewer means find the difference: 9 − 5 = 4. (Adding gives 14, but that is how many altogether.)

items.q: Which column shows 10 books?
items.e: Find 10 on the side. Go across the line for 10. The Mia column ends on that line.

items.q: How many more shells did Grace find than Kai?
items.e: Grace: 6. Kai: 1. How many more means find the difference: 6 − 1 = 5. (Adding gives 7, but that is how many altogether.)

items.q: How many birds did the class see altogether?
items.e: Read every column: Magpie 2, Lorikeet 6, Galah 1, Ibis 8. Add them: 2 + 6 + 1 + 8 = 17 birds.

items.q: Which column shows the most students?
items.e: The tallest column shows the most. The Bike column is 6 high.

items.q: How many more students have a cat than a bird?
items.e: Cat: 5. Bird: 2. How many more means find the difference: 5 − 2 = 3. (Adding gives 7, but that is how many altogether.)

items.q: How many votes did the emu and the echidna get altogether?
items.e: Emu: 8. Echidna: 3. Altogether means add: 8 + 3 = 11 votes. (5 is the difference.)

items.q: Table: Red 5, Blue 7, Pink 3, Green 6. Which column graph shows the same data as the table?
items.e: Check every column against the table: Red 5, Blue 7, Pink 3, Green 6. C matches every number. A: two columns are the wrong way round; B: one column is 1 too tall; D: one column is 1 too short.

items.q: Tally table: Dog 1 group of 5 and 1 mark, Cat 4 marks, Fish 2 marks, Bird 1 group of 5. Which column graph shows the same data as the tally table?
items.e: First count the tallies: Dog 6, Cat 4, Fish 2, Bird 5. Check every column against the table: Dog 6, Cat 4, Fish 2, Bird 5. A matches every number. B: two columns are the wrong way round; C: one column is 1 too tall; D: one column is 1 too short.
Check every row against the table: Apple 4, Kiwi 6, Plum 5, Pear 2. D matches every number. A: one row has 1 picture too few; B: two rows are the wrong way round; C: one row has 1 picture too many.

items.q: Tally table: Magpie 1 group of 5 and 1 mark, Galah 3 marks, Ibis 1 group of 5. Which picture graph shows the same data as the tally table?
items.e: First count the tallies: Magpie 6, Galah 3, Ibis 5. Check every row against the table: Magpie 6, Galah 3, Ibis 5. B matches every number. A: one row has 1 picture too many; C: two rows are the wrong way round; D: one row has 1 picture too few.

items.q: The tally table and the column graph show the same data. How tall should the missing column for Banana be?
items.e: Read the Banana row of the tally table. 1 group of 5 and 4 more. Count 5, then 6, 7, 8, 9. So it is 9. Draw the Banana column up to the line for 9.

items.q: The tally table and the column graph show the same data. How tall should the missing column for Zara be?
items.e: Read the Zara row of the tally table. 2 groups of 5. Count 5, 10. So it is 10. Draw the Zara column up to the line for 10.

items.q: The tally table and the column graph show the same data. How tall should the missing column for Oliver be?
items.e: Read the Oliver row of the tally table. 1 group of 5 and 1 more. Count 5, then 6. So it is 6. Draw the Oliver column up to the line for 6.

items.q: The tally table and the column graph show the same data. How tall should the missing column for Car be?
items.e: Read the Car row of the tally table. 2 groups of 5 and 1 more. Count 5, 10, then 11. So it is 11. Draw the Car column up to the line for 11.

items.q: How many more students chose netball than cricket?
items.e: Netball 9, cricket 5. How many more means take away: 9 − 5 = 4. (14 is 9 + 5.)

items.q: How many students chose AFL or soccer?
items.e: AFL 8, soccer 6. AFL or soccer means add: 8 + 6 = 14. (2 is the difference.)

items.q: Every student in 2A voted once. How many students are in 2A?
items.e: Read every column: 8, 5, 9, 6 and 3. Add them: 8 + 5 + 9 + 6 + 3 = 31. (9 is only the tallest column.)

items.q: Which sentence is true?
c: Soccer got more votes than AFL.
Netball got 1 more vote than AFL.
items.e: Netball 9 and AFL 8, so netball got 1 more. Swim (3) was the least popular. Soccer (6) is less than AFL (8). Cricket got 5; 6 is soccer.

items.q: The teacher picks the two most popular sports for sport day. Which two?
items.e: The two tallest columns are netball (9) and AFL (8). Soccer is next with 6.

items.q: How many more oranges than bananas were sold?
items.e: Oranges 9, bananas 4. How many more means take away: 9 − 4 = 5. (13 is 9 + 4.)

items.q: How many apples and mangoes were sold altogether?
items.e: Apples 7, mangoes 2. Altogether means add: 7 + 2 = 9. (5 is the difference.)

items.q: How many pieces of fruit were sold altogether?
items.e: Count every row: 7, 4, 9, 2. Add them: 7 + 4 + 9 + 2 = 22. (Leaving out mango gives 20.)

items.q: Tomorrow the canteen sells 3 more mangoes. How many mangoes is that tomorrow?
items.e: Today: 2 mangoes. 3 more means add: 2 + 3 = 5 mangoes.

items.q: Grace made a tally table and a column graph of the same votes. Cricket has 2 groups of 5 and 1 more mark. How tall should the cricket column be?
items.e: Count the tally: 5, 10, then 11. The column must also show 11. (Counting each group as 4 gives 9.)

items.q: Lachlan says, “Koala got more votes than kangaroo and wombat together.” Is he right?
c: No. Kangaroo and wombat got 10, which is 1 more.
Yes. Koala has the most votes.
items.e: Kangaroo and wombat together: 6 + 4 = 10. Koala: 9. 10 is more than 9, so Lachlan is wrong.

items.q: Ethan wants to show his class which fruit got the most votes. Which display shows this most quickly?
items.e: In a column graph you can see the tallest column at once. With a list of every vote you must count each fruit first.
